name: British Columbia
note: In British Columbia the funeral director drives registration. Within 48 hours the certifier gives the funeral director a medical certificate, often electronic (PEMCOD/eMCOD). The funeral director takes the deceased's particulars from the next of kin and promptly lodges both with a vital statistics registrar, who registers the death and issues the disposition permit that burial and cremation require. Each month the registrar general sends registered deaths to the chief electoral officer, and shares data with public agencies under s. 41.1 agreements. Provincial deaths reach the federal SIN program and the CRA without family action. Private bodies have no official route.

steps.title: Physician or nurse practitioner attends an expected death
steps.who: The attending physician or nurse practitioner; for an expected home death, by completing an Expected Death at Home form in advance.
steps.summary: The Vital Statistics Act has no separate pronouncement rule. Provincial guidance says the physician or coroner decides when the body can be moved. Where a physician or nurse practitioner completed an Expected Death at Home form, the funeral home can remove the body without involving a coroner.

steps.title: Report a reportable death to a coroner
steps.who: Any person with reason to believe the death was violent, accidental, self-inflicted, sudden and unexpected, untreated, pregnancy-related, or in a prescribed class. Also a funeral director, physician or nurse practitioner where no practitioner attended or no certificate can be signed within 48 hours.
steps.trigger: Reason to believe the death falls in a reportable class.
steps.summary: Everyone has a duty to report a reportable death immediately to a coroner or peace officer. The Vital Statistics Act adds a duty on funeral directors and practitioners to notify the coroner when no practitioner attended the last illness or when the certificate cannot be completed within 48 hours.

steps.title: Complete the medical certificate of death
steps.who: The medical practitioner or nurse practitioner who attended the last illness (or who has a coroner's consent for a natural death), or the coroner who investigates.
steps.summary: The certifier completes the medical certificate, with the cause of death under the WHO classification, and makes it available to the funeral director within 48 hours. Physicians and nurse practitioners can certify electronically (PEMCOD) and coroners through eMCOD. If the cause is pending, an interim certificate is issued and the final one goes to the registrar general later.

steps.title: Informant gives the deceased's personal particulars to the funeral director
steps.who: In order: the nearest relative present at the death or last illness; any relative; an adult present at the death; another adult with knowledge; the occupier of the premises; the coroner.
steps.summary: BC registration runs through the funeral director. On the funeral director's request, the first available informant in the statutory order supplies the deceased's personal particulars in the registrar general's form.

steps.title: Funeral director delivers statement and certificate for registration
steps.who: The funeral director, to a vital statistics registrar (a Service BC office or the Vital Statistics Agency).
steps.trigger: Receipt of both the statement of particulars and the medical (or interim) certificate.

deadline.text: promptly; the registrar may register only within one year of death, after which the registrar general must be applied to

steps.summary: The funeral director must promptly deliver the statement and certificate to a vital statistics registrar, who registers the death if satisfied. Where the coroner used eMCOD, the funeral director completes registration in that system. Failing to furnish a required statement in time is an offence (fine up to $50,000). Without a funeral home, a family can register at Service BC.

steps.title: Registrar issues the disposition permit
steps.trigger: Receipt of the statement and certificate.
steps.summary: Registration gates disposal. The registrar issues a disposition permit, and no one may bury, cremate or remove the body from the community without it. Cemetery and crematorium operators must hold the permit, and cremation cannot take place within 48 hours of death.

steps.title: Registrar general issues death certificates and certified copies
steps.who: Death certificate (no cause of death): any person who applies with satisfactory information and pays the fee. Certified copy of the registration: only the nearest relative, a doctor treating a family member, a court-authorized person, a government officer, anyone after 20 years, or a person showing good faith.
steps.summary: BC's access is two-tier. The short death certificate is available to any applicant who satisfies the registrar general. The certified copy of the registration, which carries more detail, is limited to listed persons. Cause of death is withheld except by deputy-minister authority or court order.

steps.title: Registrar general sends monthly death lists to the chief electoral officer
steps.who: The registrar general, to BC's chief electoral officer.
steps.trigger: Death registrations since the previous list.
steps.summary: Every month the registrar general must send the chief electoral officer the names and addresses of people whose deaths were registered since the last list. On request, the registrar general must also search the death register to resolve objections to a voter's registration.

steps.title: Registrar general shares registered deaths with benefit and record agencies
steps.who: The registrar general, under information-sharing agreements with BC, other-provincial or federal agencies and ministries (e.g. Canada Pension, Workers' Compensation, BC Cancer Agency).
steps.summary: Death registrations may be disclosed in bulk or on a regular basis under information-sharing agreements. For death data shared with a government agency to verify its records or decide entitlement to a benefit, no ministerial approval is needed. The Vital Statistics Agency says registrations update voter lists, Canada Pension, Workers' Compensation and the BC Cancer Agency.

steps.title: Vital Statistics Agency notifies the federal SIN program
steps.who: The BC Vital Statistics Agency, to ESDC's Social Insurance Register (see ca-federal).
steps.summary: BC is a province, so ESDC's statement that provincial vital statistics agencies notify the SIN program automatically covers it. BC was also among the provinces sending death data directly to the CRA (see ca-federal).

steps.title: Death registrations feed provincial and national mortality statistics
steps.who: The registrar general (provincial statistics and annual report) and, through national standards, Statistics Canada.
steps.summary: The registrar general publishes death statistics and an annual report. The Agency says certification data are the basis for both provincial and national mortality statistics, using Statistics Canada and WHO standards.

steps.title: Personal representative may advertise for creditors in the Gazette

deadline.text: claims period of at least 30 days from publication

steps.summary: BC has no general public notice of death. The personal representative may publish a notice to creditors in the BC Gazette. After the claims period ends, the representative may distribute the estate and is protected from claims not presented.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: No fixed day count. The certificate is due within 48 hours, the funeral director must deliver 'promptly', and disposal is impossible without the permit that registration produces. A local registrar can register only within one year.

informantDuty.note: Relatives (then others, in a statutory order) supply the particulars, but only on the funeral director's request. The funeral director carries the duty to deliver them for registration.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No independent review of non-coroner certificates. Coroner involvement depends on reporting duties.

electronicRegistration.note: Physicians and nurse practitioners can certify through PEMCOD and coroners through eMCOD, which the funeral director uses to complete registration. Paper forms remain in use.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No population register. The registrar general holds the vital statistics register and shares it under agreements.

governmentPropagation.note: The registrar general sends monthly death lists to the chief electoral officer and shares data with agencies under s. 41.1 agreements. Provincial deaths reach the federal SIN program and the CRA automatically. Families are still asked to notify some programs, such as CPP/OAS.

certificateAccess.note: Any person may obtain a death certificate (without cause of death). Certified copies of the registration are restricted to listed persons, or open to anyone after 20 years.

privateSectorVerification.note: Information-sharing agreements are limited to public bodies, and vital statistics information is otherwise confidential. Private bodies rely on a certificate from the family.

gaps: No statutory rule on who may pronounce death in BC was found in the Vital Statistics Act or Coroners Act. Nurse and paramedic pronouncement is presumably governed by professional standards or Ministry of Health policy, which were not searched; the Expected Death at Home form process was taken from provincial guidance only.

The individual s. 41.1 information-sharing agreements (with ESDC, CRA, the Medical Services Plan, ICBC) were not found published. Whether MSP (health insurance) and ICBC (driver licensing) are updated automatically was not established.
Elections BC's own Election Act provisions on using the registrar general's monthly death list were not read.
The Statistics Canada data-supply agreement with the BC Vital Statistics Agency was not found; national mortality statistics are sourced to the Agency's handbook only.
The Vital Statistics Act regulations (B.C. Reg. 553/82 and later) were not read, so any prescribed time for the funeral director beyond 'promptly' is unconfirmed.
